papers.what_it_is: The original quantum annealing paper: it solves the Schrödinger equation of an 8-spin transverse Ising model with a decreasing transverse field and compares ground-state probability with a classical master-equation simulated annealing. It also gives exact single-spin solutions for three schedules.

assertions.value: The authors propose quantum annealing, in which the transverse field Γ(t) is decreased from a very large value to zero so that quantum tunneling causes transitions between states, in place of the thermal transitions of simulated annealing. The target is the ground state of the classical part H0.
assertions.anchor: Section II, p.3; Section II, p.4
quotes: By decreasing the amplitude Γ(t) of the transverse ﬁeld from a very large value to zero, we hopefully drive the system into the optimal state, the ground state of
The corresponding process in QA should be to change Γ(t) from a very large value to zero.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section II defines the Hamiltonian and the annealing protocol.

assertions.value: The authors compare the two methods by numerically solving the time-dependent Schrödinger equation for QA and the classical master equation for SA, which uses single-spin-flip transitions. Both are solved for small systems with the same exchange interactions and the same annealing schedules.
quotes: We solve the time-dependent Schr¨odinger equation and the classical master equation numerically for small-size systems
We consider single-spin ﬂip processes with the transition matrix elements given as
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own simulation method in the Introduction and Section II.

assertions.value: The authors state that only small systems of N = 8 spins were treated, so the ground state can be picked out explicitly, and that all calculations used a constant longitudinal field h = 0.1 to remove trivial degeneracy.
assertions.anchor: Section II, p.4; Section III, p.4
quotes: Note that we treat only small-size systems (the number of spins N = 8)
All calculations were performed with a constant longitudinal ﬁeld h = 0.1 to remove trivial degeneracy.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the system size and field value used for all numerical results.
assertions.reader_inference: All numerical QA-versus-SA comparisons are therefore for N = 8 only.

assertions.value: The authors report that QA converges to the ground state with larger probability than SA in all the cases tested when the same annealing schedule is used. The abstract says 'almost all cases'.
quotes: We have found that QA shows convergence to the optimal (ground) state with larger probability than SA in all cases if the same annealing schedule is used.
the quantum annealing leads to the ground state with much larger probability in almost all cases
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from small N = 8 numerical solutions in one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract's 'almost all cases' and the summary's 'in all cases' differ slightly; the text discusses cases where both methods fail (3/t) and one where the QA curves lie below SA (log schedule).

assertions.value: For the ferromagnetic model with Γ(t) = T(t) = 3/log(t + 1), the authors report that both QA and SA follow their quasi-static states rather accurately and that the numerical data indicate PQA converges to the ground state.
quotes: Figure 1 shows the overlaps for the case of
both QA and SA follow stationary (equilibrium) states during dynamical processes rather
the numerical data
indicate convergence to the ground state under the annealing schedule Γ(t) = 3/ log(t + 1)
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one numerical study; Figure 1 was not viewable.

assertions.value: The authors state that there are no mathematically rigorous arguments for QA corresponding to the Geman-Geman bound, so convergence of QA under this schedule rests on numerical data for the ferromagnetic system.
quotes: Although there are no mathematically rigorous arguments for QA corresponding to the Geman-Geman bound, the numerical data
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit of their own numerical evidence.

assertions.value: The authors state that the unit of time is arbitrary (ħ = 1 in the Schrödinger equation and the unit of time τ = 1 in the master equation), so QA curves lying below SA curves at a given time under the log schedule has no positive significance.
quotes: It should be remembered that the unit of time is
does not have any positive signiﬁcance.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit on how the time axes of QA and SA can be compared.
assertions.reader_inference: Time comparisons between QA and SA curves are not meaningful in absolute terms; comparisons are about asymptotic convergence.

assertions.value: For the ferromagnetic model with Γ(t) = T(t) = 3 over the square root of t, the authors report that QA converges to the ground state clearly better than SA, which gets stuck in a local minimum with non-negligible probability.
quotes: Γ(t) = T (t) = 3/ t, there appears a qualitative
The quantum method clearly gives better convergence to the ground state while the classical counterpart
gets stuck in a local minimum with a non-negligible probability.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one small-system numerical study; Figure 2 was not viewable.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the ferromagnetic model with Γ(t) = 3 over the square root of t, 1 − PQA behaves as const/t in the time region between 100 and 1000.
quotes: It is seen that 1 − PQA behaves as const/t in the time region between 100 and 1000.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result read from a log-log plot over one decade of time.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 3: on log-log axes 1−PQA stays near 1 up to t of about 10, then falls to about 0.2 at t of about 100 and about 0.02 at t of about 1000. Between about 100 and about 1000 the solid curve runs parallel to the dotted 1/t guide line.
quotes: we have plotted 1 − PQA in a log-log scale in Fig. 3
The dotted line represents t−1 to guide the eye.
assertions.certainty_reason: A value read by eye from one plot.
assertions.reader_inference: The slope is about −1, consistent with the 1/t statement in the text.

assertions.value: For the ferromagnetic model with the faster schedule Γ(t) = T(t) = 3/t, the authors report that the system becomes trapped in intermediate states in both QA and SA.
quotes: By a still faster annealing schedule Γ(t) = T (t) = 3/t
the system becomes trapped in intermediate states both in QA and SA
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one numerical study; Figure 4 was not viewable.
assertions.reader_inference: QA's advantage disappears when the field is decreased too fast.

assertions.value: The frustrated test model has solid lines for ferromagnetic interactions and a broken line for an antiferromagnetic interaction of the same absolute value as the ferromagnetic ones. The authors argue that the correlation of spins 3 and 6 changes sign as temperature is decreased, so the free-energy landscape restructures during annealing.
quotes: The full lines indicate ferromagnetic interactions while the broken line is for an antiferromagnetic
interaction with the same absolute value as the ferromagnetic ones.
Therefore the spins 3 and 6 must change their relative orientation at some intermediate temperature.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors define the frustrated model and its design rationale in Section III.B.

assertions.value: The authors report that the classical correlation of spins 3 and 6 is negative at high temperature and positive at low temperature. They state that the quantum correlation as a function of Γ shows a similar dependence, supporting the identification of Γ with T.
quotes: This argument is justiﬁed by the positive value of the correlation function at low temperatures in Fig. 6.
The broken curve in Fig. 6 clearly supports this idea.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one small numerical study; Figure 6 was not viewable and this is taken from the text.

assertions.value: For the frustrated model with Γ(t) = T(t) = 3 over the square root of t, the authors report that QA is better suited than SA for ground-state search.
quotes: The tendency is clear that QA is better suited for ground-state search in the present system.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one numerical study with N = 8; Figure 7 was not viewable.

assertions.value: For the 8-spin SK model, the authors draw couplings from a Gaussian with zero mean and variance 1/N and use Γ(t) = T(t) = 3 over the square root of t. They report that a typical realization shows QA better suited than SA, and that several other realizations gave qualitatively the same results.
quotes: Interactions exist between all pairs of spins and are chosen from a Gaussian distribution with vanishing mean and variance 1/N (N = 8 in our case).
have found that the results are qualitatively the same.
Figure 8 again suggests that QA is better suited than SA for the present optimization problem.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from a few random N = 8 instances; Figure 8 was not viewable.
assertions.reader_inference: Only 'several realizations' are mentioned and no statistics are given.

assertions.value: For the Landau-Zener schedule Γ(t) = −ct on a single spin, the authors derive an exact solution. For h squared over c much greater than 1, the ground-state probability at t = 0 falls short of 1 by an amount of order c squared over h to the fourth power. They conclude that PQA does not approach 1 for finite c.
assertions.anchor: Section IV, p.6; p.7; Appendix, p.10
quotes: Let us ﬁrst discuss the case of Γ(t) = −ct with t changing from −∞ to 0.
The probability to ﬁnd the system in the ground state at t = 0 is, when h2/c ≫ 1,
Thus the probability PQA(t) does not approach 1 for ﬁnite c.
assertions.certainty_reason: An analytical result derived in Section IV and the Appendix; the formula is garbled in the text layer, so the order is given in words.

assertions.value: For the schedule Γ(t) = c/t on a single spin with initial condition a = b = 1/√2, the authors derive the exact solution and an asymptotic form. They report that the system does not reach the ground state as t → ∞ for finite c, and that for c ≫ 1 the asymptotic probability is 1 − e−2πc.
quotes: the last approximation being valid for c ≫ 1 after t → ∞.
The system does not reach the ground state as t → ∞ as long as c is ﬁnite.
assertions.certainty_reason: An analytical derivation in Section IV and Appendix part 2.

assertions.value: For the schedule Γ(t) = c/√t on a single spin, the authors derive the exact solution with initial condition a = b = 1/√2 and an asymptotic probability for c² / h ≫ 1 that falls short of 1 by an amount of order h² / c⁴ (written as 64c⁴ in the paper). They conclude that the ground state is not reached perfectly for any of the three schedules.
assertions.anchor: Section IV, p.8; Section V, p.8
quotes: and the probability PQA(∞) for c2/h ≫ 1 is obtained as
The results showed that the ground state is not reached perfectly for all these annealing schedules.
assertions.certainty_reason: An analytical result in Section IV and the Appendix; the formula is garbled in the text layer, so it is described by order only.

assertions.value: The authors state that the asymptotic values of PQA(t) in their numerical calculations are probably not exactly 1, although they seem quite close to the optimal value 1.
quotes: Therefore the asymptotic values of PQA(t) in numerical calculations are probably not exactly 1 although they seem to be quite close to the optimal value 1.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit on their numerical convergence claim, based on the single-spin solutions.

assertions.value: The authors show that, for Γ(t) = c/√t, an appropriate choice of initial condition drives the system to the ground state, and that this is not possible for any initial condition when Γ(t) = −ct or c/t.
quotes: possible for any initial conditions in the case of Γ(t) = −ct or c/t.
We show that we can choose the initial condition so that the ﬁnal state is the ground
assertions.certainty_reason: Derived analytically in Appendix part 4.
assertions.reader_inference: The authors note the resulting initial state is not the ground state of H(0), so this does not give a practical protocol.

assertions.value: Using perturbation theory in Γ and assuming the system follows quasi-static states, the authors argue that for Γ = c/√t the approach of PQA to its asymptotic value is proportional to 1/t. They state that the corresponding SA probability shows no universal 1/t-like dependence on time.
quotes: Thus the approach to the asymptotic value is proportional to 1/t as long as the system stays in quasi-static states.
which shows absence of universal (1/t-like) dependence on time.
assertions.certainty_reason: A simple perturbative argument that assumes quasi-static following.
assertions.reader_inference: The authors note that the single-spin solution contains a 1/√t term, and suggest its coefficient is very small in the ferromagnetic case.

assertions.value: The authors suggest that the transverse field represents a transition rate larger than the SA transition rate at the same small control parameter, and that this larger transition probability may lead to a more active search in wider regions of phase space and better convergence.
quotes: This larger transition probability may lead to a more active search in wider regions of the phase space, leading to
better convergence similarly to the case of the generalized transition probability.
assertions.certainty_reason: A heuristic explanation offered without a test in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that their direct numerical method faces difficulties for larger N because the number of states grows exponentially as 2^N. They also state that the reduction of computational complexity that Monte Carlo gives SA is lacking in QA, an important future problem.
quotes: The corresponding reduction of the computational complexity is lacking in QA
it is an important future problem in practical implementation of the idea of QA.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limitation of their approach.

assertions.value: The authors state as a future problem that QA must be implemented for other optimization problems, such as the travelling salesman problem or graph bipartitioning, for which there seems to be no direct analogue of the transverse field.
quotes: Another future problem is to devise implementations of QA in other optimization problems such as the travelling salesman problem
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state an open problem in the Summary and Discussions.

assertions.value: The authors cite Geman and Geman as showing that any system reaches the global minimum asymptotically if the temperature is decreased as T = c/log t or slower, with c determined by the system size and cost-function structure.
quotes: if the temperature is decreased as T = c/ log t or slower
where c is a constant determined by the system size and other structures of the cost function.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.
